I need to decide how to exit jail. I can pay the $50 fine, roll for doubles, or use a get-out-of-jail card.

I have a Get Out of Jail Free card and $360 cash. I own four houses on the dark blues and a mortgaged railroad. Opponent p1 has $531 and owns dark blues plus reds with a hotel on Boardwalk.

p4 has $439 and a light blue monopoly with four houses each. p3 is bankrupt. This appears to be my second jail decision.

I rolled 2 and 3 on my first attempt and failed to get out. Leaving jail now would send me toward dangerous properties. I can sell houses and mortgages for roughly $1180, but that still falls short of the $1300 rent on Park Place with four houses or the $2000 rent on Boardwalk with its hotel.

Leaving jail would land me on St. Charles Place, States Avenue, Virginia Avenue, and Tennessee Avenue. All are safe since I own them. The other spaces from the Jail space are mostly mortgaged or occupied by opponents.

A normal roll from jail lands on spaces 12 through 22. That range covers Electric Company, States Avenue, Virginia Avenue, and Chance. It does not include dangerous properties like Park Place or Boardwalk.

Rolling 11 from jail lands on Kentucky Avenue with one house, costing $90. That is well within my $360 cash. I am now weighing whether to roll for doubles or simply pay the fine.

Rolling doubles from jail is completely safe. Every possible double outcome lands on a mortgaged or owned property, and none of the dangerous reds are reachable.

Leaving jail would also expose me to Chance cards. A normal roll from the Jail space lands on Chance exactly 12 spaces away, and some cards advance directly to Boardwalk or Illinois Avenue. The main concern is simply re-entering the game.

p4 is now on Boardwalk after paying $1700. From there, p4 can roll toward my pink properties and land on them. I am calculating the exact landing spots from Boardwalk.

From Boardwalk, rolling 12 spaces lands on St. Charles Place with four houses. The rent is $625. That is a major threat.

Virginia Avenue also charges $625 with four houses. p4 has $439, so landing there would bankrupt them or force them to mortgage or sell houses. The turn order is now clear: I act first, then p4, then p1, then I return. If I stay in jail, p4 will roll from Boardwalk and p1 from North Carolina.

p1 cannot land on my pink properties from North Carolina this turn. The required roll would be nineteen or higher, which is impossible.

p4 can only reach St. Charles Place from Boardwalk by rolling twelve.

Neither opponent poses an immediate threat to my pinks while I remain in jail.

I will stay in jail. p1 is too far away to reach my pink properties this turn, and p4 can only land on St. Charles Place from Boardwalk by rolling doubles, which is unlikely this turn.

I am now calculating the exact cash needed to survive the rent on Park Place and Boardwalk. Selling all four houses on my pink properties would return roughly six hundred dollars, but mortgaging them first yields only about two hundred dollars in total. That is still far below the one thousand three hundred dollars for Park Place or two thousand dollars for Boardwalk.

Liquidating all houses and mortgages yields only $1180. That is still $120 short of the $1300 rent on Park Place with four houses, and far below the $2000 rent on Boardwalk with its hotel. I am dead if I land on either property. I must stay in jail until those properties are stripped.

I am now checking whether p4 can be forced to strip their own houses. Their light blue properties could cover a $625 pink rent, but they would need to sell houses or mortgage railroads.

The win condition is forcing p1 to sell their dark blue houses or hotel to pay pink rent. p1 has $531, which is enough to cover a $625 pink rent. p4's light blue properties charge about $400 with four houses. p1 is nineteen spaces away from St. Charles Place, so they cannot land there this turn.

I have already spent one turn in jail. Standard Monopoly rules allow three double rolls before the fine or a get-out-of-jail card is mandatory.

I will roll for doubles. I am keeping my Get Out of Jail Free card for later, and paying the fine would waste cash I might need. Rolling doubles gives a one-in-six chance to leave safely.

I am reconsidering whether rolling doubles from jail grants another roll. Standard Monopoly rules say a doubles roll to leave jail ends the turn immediately, so I would not get a second roll.

I will roll for doubles. I am drafting a calm public message to avoid revealing my cash weakness or my reason for staying in jail.

I will keep my public message short and avoid clever phrasing. I am updating my strategy notes for future reference.

p1 now owns a Boardwalk hotel, four houses on Park Place, and a red monopoly. They paid $1700 to p4 and still have $531 in cash after building. This makes them more dangerous.

p4 paid $1700 but still has $439. They survived the hotel purchase without going bankrupt.

p4 paid $1700 for four houses on Boardwalk, not the hotel. The hotel upgrade happened on p1's turn 155 after that payment. p4 is currently on Boardwalk and has already paid.

The light blue properties are not an immediate threat from jail. They sit behind me at spaces 6, 8, and 9. Leaving jail would require almost a full circuit before those could be reached.

I am now weighing the immediate dangers if I exit jail and continue moving forward.

The bank has no houses left. p1 built a hotel on Boardwalk and used the returned houses to upgrade reds, so they likely have enough cash to keep building. I will stay in jail.

p1 might upgrade Park Place to a hotel. That would return four houses to the bank and let them build more reds. I will stay in jail to prevent that.

Staying in jail does not stop p1 from building. It only prevents me from landing on improved properties.

p4 already owns four houses on each light blue. They can buy hotels there because hotels do not require bank houses. That would return four houses to the bank. Those freed houses could let p1 build reds or other properties.

Reds with two houses cost $300, which I can afford. Three houses would raise rent to $700–$750, killing me. p1 could hotel Park Place for $200, freeing four houses that they would immediately place on reds. That would make the reds lethal before I ever reach dark blues.

Hotel Park Place would cost $200 and leave p1 with only $331. They could then add two houses to the reds for $300, raising rent to about $250–$300. That is survivable with my $360 cash, so they might not hotel PP after all. They may prefer to save that money and survive my pink rents instead.

p1 only needs to sell one house on Park Place to pay the $625 pink rent. That leaves three houses on Park Place, which is still expensive but survivable. The win path is keeping my pink properties at four houses and forcing p1 to strip one of their dark blue buildings.

If p1 strips one house from Park Place, rent drops to $1100. Full liquidation yields about $1180, leaving only $80 remaining. That is barely enough to survive. Boardwalk with its hotel still costs $2000, so that property remains fatal.

p1 can mortgage Ventnor for $130 to cover the pink rent without selling any houses. That leaves all dark blue buildings intact, so I cannot force a strip by landing on a pink property.

p1 has mortgaged most of their properties. Only Ventnor remains unmortgaged and unimproved. That $130 mortgage covers the $94 gap to pay pink rent without selling any houses. If my pinks had hotels, the rent would be $750 and they would have to sell houses instead. But the bank has no houses or hotels left for them to buy.

I cannot upgrade my pink properties to hotels right now. The current decision is a jail action, not a build action, so I have no available build action. Hotels do not require bank houses; they return four houses to the bank when purchased. If I were able to hotel later, those returned houses could let p1 build reds to lethal levels.

Hoteling my pink properties would return twelve houses to the bank. p1 could then buy five red houses for $750, raising rent to about $750 on Illinois and killing me with only $360 cash. I will stay in jail and roll for doubles.
